title: Virtual Memory & mmap
summary: Virtual memory abstracts physical RAM through a per-process address space managed by the OS and MMU hardware. Every process believes it has exclusive access to a large contiguous address space; the OS maps this virtual space to physical pages on demand. mmap() extends this model to file-backed and anonymous mappings, enabling zero-copy file I/O, shared memory IPC, and the memory-mapped file patterns used by databases, JVMs, and ML frameworks. Understanding page faults, TLB shootdowns, huge pages, and swap behavior is essential for diagnosing memory pressure and designing memory-intensive services.

sections.title: Virtual Address Space and Page Tables
paragraphs: Every process on Linux has a 64-bit virtual address space (48 bits usable on x86-64: 128 TB each for user and kernel). The OS divides this into pages—4 KB by default—which are the unit of mapping, permission, and eviction. Physical RAM is divided into page frames of the same size. The kernel maintains a page table per process: a hierarchical data structure mapping virtual page numbers to physical page frame numbers along with permission bits (read/write/execute) and status flags (present, dirty, accessed).

When the CPU translates a virtual address, it walks the page table in hardware via the MMU (Memory Management Unit). Modern x86-64 uses a 4-level page table (PGD → PUD → PMD → PTE). To avoid walking the page table on every memory access, the CPU caches recent translations in the TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer). A TLB hit is fast (1 cycle); a TLB miss triggers a page walk (10–50 cycles if the page table is in L1/L2 cache) or, if the page is not present in physical memory, a page fault (1,000–10,000,000 cycles depending on whether it's served from disk).

On a TLB miss where the page table entry exists but the physical page is not in RAM, the CPU raises a page fault. The OS page fault handler is invoked. For a minor page fault (page exists in memory, just not mapped—e.g., a copy-on-write scenario), the handler maps the page and resumes the process. For a major page fault (page must be fetched from disk or swap), the process blocks while the kernel performs I/O. Major page faults are orders of magnitude more expensive—1–10 ms of disk latency vs. <1 μs for minor faults.

Copy-on-Write (CoW) is the kernel optimization that makes fork() fast. When a process forks, the kernel doesn't copy all pages—it marks both parent and child page table entries as read-only and CoW-flagged. When either process writes to a shared page, the write triggers a page fault; the fault handler copies the page and updates the writing process's page table to point to the new copy. For a 1 GB process that writes only 10 MB after fork, CoW limits the actual copy to 10 MB—the rest is shared until modified.
bullets: Page size: 4 KB default; huge pages: 2 MB (x86-64 large pages) or 1 GB (huge pages); see /proc/meminfo
TLB: fully associative caches 1024–8192 entries on modern CPUs; thrashed by processes with large working sets
Major vs minor page fault: minor (<1μs, CoW or zero page); major (1–10ms, disk I/O)

sections.title: mmap(): File and Anonymous Mappings
paragraphs: mmap() asks the kernel to create a mapping in the calling process's address space. For file-backed mappings, the mapped region mirrors the file's bytes: reading from the region reads the file; writing to a MAP_SHARED region writes through to the file. The kernel uses the page cache as the backing store—pages already in cache are mapped directly into the process's address space without copying. This is zero-copy file I/O: a process reading 1 GB of data via mmap() with the data already in page cache performs no read syscall and copies no data—it accesses the cache pages directly through hardware page table mappings.

Anonymous mappings (MAP_ANONYMOUS) are not backed by any file—they're backed by the swap device or just zero pages. malloc() and mmap() for anonymous pages are how heap memory is allocated. For small allocations, glibc's malloc uses brk() to extend the heap; for large allocations (>MMAP_THRESHOLD, default 128 KB), malloc uses mmap() directly. mmap'd allocations are independent virtual memory regions—munmap() returns them to the OS immediately, unlike brk-grown heap which never shrinks.

MAP_SHARED vs MAP_PRIVATE determines write visibility. MAP_SHARED: writes are visible to other processes mapping the same file and are flushed to the underlying file. Used for shared memory IPC and memory-mapped databases. MAP_PRIVATE: writes are Copy-on-Write—the process gets a private copy of modified pages; writes are not visible to other processes or persisted to file. Used when you want to read a file but modify it in memory without changing the original.

msync() flushes dirty pages from the page cache to the underlying storage device. Without msync(), the kernel may defer writes for seconds or minutes (controlled by dirty_writeback_centisecs and dirty_expire_centisecs sysctls). For durability-critical writes (database WAL, checkpoint files), always call msync(MS_SYNC) or fdatasync() after writing. The difference: msync() on mmap'd regions, fsync()/fdatasync() on file descriptors—both flush to the storage device (not just page cache).
bullets: mmap MAP_POPULATE: pre-fault all pages eagerly; avoids page-fault latency during first access
madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL): hint to kernel to prefetch pages ahead; useful for sequential scan workloads
madvise(MADV_DONTNEED): release pages from memory; kernel can reclaim them; re-access causes page fault

sections.title: Page Cache and Memory Pressure
paragraphs: The Linux page cache is a unified cache for file data and anonymous pages. Every read() from a file populates the page cache; subsequent reads of the same file range are served from cache without disk I/O. The page cache grows to fill available RAM—it is not a fixed-size cache. Linux uses an LRU variant with two lists: active (recently accessed) and inactive (candidates for eviction). Pages move between lists based on access patterns. When memory pressure occurs, the kernel evicts inactive pages first.

Memory pressure signals propagate through the system. The 'available' memory in free -m is not just 'free'—it includes reclaimable page cache and slab caches. When an application allocates memory and no free pages remain, the kernel reclaims page cache pages (clean ones for free, dirty ones after writeback). This reclaim is usually invisible: the application gets its memory, and subsequent file accesses repopulate the cache from disk. When reclaim is not fast enough, the kernel invokes the OOM killer—it selects a process to kill based on heuristics (oom_score) and kills it.

Swappiness controls the kernel's tendency to swap anonymous pages to the swap device rather than reclaiming page cache. vm.swappiness=100 means 'swap anonymous pages as aggressively as reclaim file cache'; vm.swappiness=0 means 'never swap if there's reclaimable file cache'. For latency-sensitive applications (databases, caches), set swappiness to 0–10: a process that gets swapped experiences 10–100ms latency spikes when swapped pages are accessed. Many database recommendations set vm.swappiness=1 (essentially disable swap while still allowing emergency use).

Transparent Huge Pages (THP) is a Linux feature that automatically backs mappings with 2 MB pages instead of 4 KB pages. This reduces TLB pressure (1 TLB entry covers 2 MB vs 4 KB), improving throughput for large working sets. However, THP has a notorious interaction with databases and JVMs: the khugepaged daemon compacts pages into huge pages in the background, causing sporadic 10–100ms stalls. Redis, MongoDB, Oracle, and the JVM documentation all recommend disabling THP (echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled). Use explicit huge pages (HugeTLBfs) for performance-critical static allocations instead.
bullets: vm.swappiness=1: near-disable swap; recommended for Redis, Postgres, Elasticsearch
THP (Transparent Huge Pages): disable for latency-sensitive services; use HugeTLBfs explicitly for DPDK/JVM
mlock()/mlockall(): pin pages in RAM; prevent swapping; requires CAP_IPC_LOCK

sections.title: Huge Pages and TLB Optimization
paragraphs: The TLB is a critical performance bottleneck for large-working-set processes. A CPU core typically has an L1 TLB for 64 entries × 4 KB = 256 KB coverage. A Java JVM heap of 32 GB would need 8 million TLB entries to cover it at 4 KB granularity—impossible. With 2 MB huge pages, 32 GB requires only 16,384 entries. Applications with large heaps or large mmap'd files benefit dramatically from huge pages: JVM throughput improvements of 10–30% are common after migrating to 2 MB huge pages.

Linux HugeTLBfs reserves huge pages at boot time. Configure with vm.nr_hugepages=N in /etc/sysctl.conf; each page is 2 MB. Applications request huge pages by mmap()ing /dev/hugepages with MAP_HUGETLB flag, or using hugetlbfs-backed files. DPDK requires huge pages (1 GB pages for NIC DMA rings); some JVM implementations (Azul, GraalVM) can use huge pages via -XX:+UseLargePages. The reservation is static—huge pages not in use by applications are unavailable to other workloads.

NUMA (Non-Uniform Memory Access) interacts with virtual memory. On multi-socket servers, each CPU socket has local RAM (fast: ~100 ns) and remote RAM (accessed via QPI/UPI: ~200–300 ns). The Linux memory allocator uses NUMA-aware allocation by default: pages are allocated from the socket-local NUMA node of the requesting CPU. If the application's thread and its data are on different NUMA nodes—common when threads migrate between sockets—memory accesses incur NUMA remote access penalties, causing 2–3× latency for memory-bound workloads.
bullets: HugeTLBfs: statically reserved; accessible via /dev/hugepages or hugetlbfs mount
numactl --membind=0 --cpunodebind=0: pin process to NUMA node 0; prevent cross-NUMA accesses
NUMA first-touch: pages allocated on node where first thread touches them; design thread binding accordingly

sections.title: Memory-Mapped Databases and mmap I/O Patterns
paragraphs: LMDB (Lightning Memory-Mapped Database), used by OpenLDAP and Symas, maps its entire database file into the process's address space with mmap(). Reads access database pages directly from the page cache without any read() syscall or memory copy. LMDB's B-tree traversal is a series of pointer dereferences through mmap'd pages—the kernel handles page-fault-driven disk reads transparently when pages are not in cache. At steady state with a hot working set, LMDB achieves near-memory-speed reads with zero syscall overhead.

The mmap I/O approach has tradeoffs. The process cannot control eviction—the OS may evict a hot database page from cache under memory pressure, causing a sudden latency spike on the next access. With read() I/O, the application controls caching explicitly (keeping frequently accessed data in a user-space cache). For this reason, PostgreSQL and RocksDB use read() I/O rather than mmap: they want explicit control over what stays in their buffer pool. The 2022 'Are You Sure You Want to Use MMAP in Your Database Management System?' paper documents this in detail.

Memory-mapped files are ideal for read-mostly workloads with large datasets where the working set fits in RAM. ML model inference: a 70B parameter model (140 GB in bfloat16) can be mmap()'d, and the inference engine accesses only the layers it needs for a given input—the kernel pages in only the accessed layers. For an 8-layer transformer inference request that only touches 20 GB, the application uses 20 GB of RAM even though the model file is 140 GB. This is the foundation of llama.cpp and similar memory-efficient inference engines.
bullets: LMDB: entire database mmap'd; reads are pointer dereferences; no buffer pool management needed
mmap vs read() for databases: mmap gives OS control of eviction; read() gives application control of buffer pool
llama.cpp: uses mmap for model weights; loads only needed layers; enables 70B inference on 24 GB RAM

core.title: Virtual Memory and Page Tables
paragraphs: Virtual address space is divided into 4 KB pages. The MMU walks a 4-level page table to translate virtual → physical addresses, caching results in the TLB. TLB miss: 10–50 cycles. Page fault: 1 μs (minor) to 10 ms (major/disk).
Copy-on-Write (fork() optimization): parent and child share pages marked read-only until one writes; write triggers page copy. Only modified pages are duplicated.
Huge pages (2 MB) reduce TLB pressure for large working sets; 10–30% JVM throughput improvement is typical.
bullets: 4-level page table on x86-64: PGD → PUD → PMD → PTE
Minor page fault: CoW or zero-fill; <1μs; major page fault: disk I/O; 1–10ms
mlock(): pin pages in RAM; prevents major page faults at runtime cost of fixed memory

core.title: mmap() Semantics
paragraphs: File-backed mmap() gives zero-copy access to the page cache. The process reads file data as memory accesses; no read() syscall or copy needed. MAP_SHARED writes persist to file; MAP_PRIVATE writes are CoW.
madvise() hints guide prefetching and eviction: MADV_SEQUENTIAL triggers readahead; MADV_DONTNEED releases pages; MADV_WILLNEED prefaults.
msync(MS_SYNC) flushes mmap'd dirty pages to storage; required for durability before crash.
bullets: MAP_POPULATE: pre-fault all pages at mmap() time; avoids latency spikes during first access
MAP_HUGETLB: request huge page backing; requires pre-reserved HugeTLBfs pages
mremap(): resize an existing mapping in place; avoids unmap/remap copying

core.title: Page Cache, Swappiness, and THP
paragraphs: Linux page cache fills available RAM. When memory pressure occurs, inactive file cache is evicted first; anonymous pages are swapped based on vm.swappiness.
vm.swappiness=1: near-disable swap; prevents latency spikes from swapped database or cache pages.
THP causes background compaction stalls; disable for latency-sensitive services. Use explicit HugeTLBfs for performance-critical allocations.
bullets: echo never > /sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled: disable THP
OOM killer: invoked when reclaim fails; oom_score_adj=-1000 protects critical processes
vm.overcommit_memory=2: prevent overcommit; prevents OOM but may cause allocation failures

deepDive.title: TLB Shootdowns and NUMA Memory Latency
paragraphs: When the kernel modifies a page table entry—unmapping a page, changing permissions, fork CoW—it must invalidate the TLB entries on all CPUs that might be caching the old translation. This requires sending an IPI (Inter-Processor Interrupt) to all CPUs, an operation called a TLB shootdown. Each shootdown takes ~1–5 μs per CPU core involved. At 100k shootdowns/second with 32 CPUs: 3.2 ms/second of CPU time wasted on shootdowns. Workloads with frequent mmap()/munmap() cycles (e.g., per-request mmap allocation) or frequent fork() incur significant TLB shootdown overhead.

NUMA memory placement is determined at first access (first-touch policy). A common mistake: allocate a large array in a main thread on NUMA node 0, then process it with threads that migrate to NUMA node 1. All accesses from node 1 threads hit remote NUMA—2–3× higher latency. Fix: pre-touch memory on the thread that will use it, or use numactl --interleave to distribute pages across NUMA nodes (better for uniform access patterns). Tools: numastat (shows per-node allocation), perf mem (shows NUMA hit/miss rates per instruction).

Memory bandwidth saturation is the hidden bottleneck in memory-bound workloads. A single DDR4 channel provides ~25 GB/s; a typical server with 4 channels has 100 GB/s. A process that does random 64-byte accesses across 100 GB working set saturates DRAM bandwidth at ~300 million accesses/second—not the DRAM latency, the bandwidth. This is why memory-bound workloads benefit from NUMA local access (keeping data close to the CPU processing it) and why compressing data (reducing working set size) can improve throughput for memory-bound systems.
bullets: TLB shootdown: IPI to all CPUs holding stale TLB entries; ~1–5μs per CPU; costly at high frequency
numactl --interleave=all: round-robin page allocation across NUMA nodes; best for uniform multi-threaded access
perf mem record + report: shows NUMA remote access fraction per memory instruction

deepDive.title: Memory-Mapped I/O in Databases and ML Inference
paragraphs: RocksDB uses a block cache (user-space LRU cache of decompressed 4–64 KB blocks) rather than mmap() for its SST files. This gives RocksDB explicit control over eviction: it can pin index and filter blocks (small, high-value) while evicting data blocks under memory pressure. mmap() would give this control to the OS page cache, which uses generic LRU without application-specific knowledge. For scan-heavy workloads (analytical queries), mmap() with MADV_SEQUENTIAL is competitive; for point-lookup-heavy workloads, explicit buffer management wins.

PyTorch and JAX use mmap() to load model checkpoints into shared memory. When multiple inference workers load the same model (common in serving with multiple process workers), the OS shares the underlying page cache pages—each worker's mmap'd address space points to the same physical pages. 10 inference workers loading the same 10 GB model share 10 GB of RAM rather than consuming 100 GB. The same sharing works for multi-GPU setups where CPU-side model copies are shared before being copied to GPU VRAM.

Fault tolerance pattern: checkpoint files written via mmap() with MAP_SHARED require msync(MS_SYNC) before the checkpoint is considered durable. Without msync, a crash between write and sync leaves a partial checkpoint on disk. The pattern: write new checkpoint to a tmp file, msync, then rename() atomically to the final path. rename() is atomic at the filesystem level—readers either see the old or new complete checkpoint, never a partial one.
bullets: PyTorch shared memory: torch.multiprocessing + mmap enables zero-copy tensor sharing between workers
mmap checkpoint pattern: write → msync → rename (atomic); ensures readers see complete checkpoints
madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE): request THP backing for specific regions; avoids khugepaged daemon overhead

expert.title: Virtual Memory at Hyperscale and Container Environments
paragraphs: In containers, virtual memory behavior depends on cgroup memory limits. When a container's cgroup memory limit is reached, the cgroup triggers its own reclaim before the global OOM killer. If reclaim doesn't free enough, the cgroup's OOM killer kills a process within the cgroup—ideally the one that caused the OOM. Setting memory.limit_in_bytes without memory.memsw.limit_in_bytes limits RSS but not swap; the container may swap heavily without being OOM-killed. Set both limits or disable swap to prevent unexpected swapping in containers.

Memory overcommit in cloud environments: by default, Linux allows overcommit—processes can mmap() more memory than physically exists. The kernel assumes not all mapped memory is used simultaneously (true for most applications due to CoW and sparse access). With vm.overcommit_memory=0 (default), the kernel uses a heuristic allowing moderate overcommit. At hyperscale, cloud providers rely on overcommit to pack more VMs per physical host than the total VM RAM would suggest. The risk: when all VMs simultaneously try to use their allocated RAM, the host OOM-kills VMs.

userfaultfd (Linux 4.11+) allows user-space programs to handle page faults in user space. A QEMU/KVM hypervisor uses userfaultfd to handle guest page faults—when a guest accesses unmapped memory, the host user-space intercepts the fault, fetches the page from the network (live migration), and resolves it, without exposing page-fault handling to the kernel. This is also used for database on-demand page loading and ML model lazy loading where the application wants custom eviction and prefetching logic beyond madvise hints.

concepts: Virtual address space: per-process 64-bit address space; mapped to physical pages by kernel page tables
MMU page walk: hardware traverses 4-level page table on TLB miss; 10–50 cycles if cached
TLB (Translation Lookaside Buffer): cache of recent virtual→physical translations; miss triggers page walk
Page fault: minor (CoW/zero-fill, <1μs) vs major (disk I/O, 1–10ms); major faults are production latency events
mmap(): creates memory mapping—file-backed (page cache) or anonymous (swap); enables zero-copy file I/O
Copy-on-Write: fork() shares pages until write; write triggers page copy; makes fork() O(dirty-pages) not O(total-memory)
Page cache: kernel's unified file data cache; fills available RAM; evicted under memory pressure
vm.swappiness: kernel preference for swapping anonymous pages vs reclaiming file cache; set low for latency-sensitive services
Transparent Huge Pages (THP): kernel-managed 2 MB page promotion; reduces TLB pressure but causes background compaction stalls
TLB shootdown: IPI to invalidate TLB entries on other CPUs after page table changes; 1–5μs/core; costly at high frequency
practices: Set vm.swappiness=1 on latency-sensitive servers (databases, caches); prevents application pages from being swapped under memory pressure
Disable THP (echo never > transparent_hugepage/enabled) for Redis, MongoDB, Postgres; use explicit huge pages if needed
Use madvise(MADV_SEQUENTIAL) for large sequential scan workloads to trigger OS readahead
Call msync(MS_SYNC) before marking checkpoints durable; mmap writes may not reach disk without explicit sync
Use mlock() / mlockall() for latency-critical processes to prevent page eviction; requires pre-sized memory and CAP_IPC_LOCK
Pin threads to NUMA nodes with numactl and allocate memory on the same node; avoid cross-NUMA remote accesses
pitfalls: Assuming 'free memory' means available memory; Linux page cache fills RAM aggressively; 'available' (not 'free') is the right metric
Using THP without testing; background compaction causes sporadic 10–100ms stalls that are hard to attribute
Forgetting msync after mmap writes; dirty pages may not reach disk for minutes without explicit sync
Setting vm.overcommit_memory=1 on production servers; allows unlimited overcommit, risking OOM killer during memory spikes
Allocating large mmap regions per request and munmap'ing immediately; each unmap triggers TLB shootdown across all CPUs
Not pre-touching huge pages before the latency-sensitive path; first access causes page faults that add measurable latency

examples.title: LMDB Zero-Copy Reads
examples.description: LMDB maps its entire database file with mmap(MAP_SHARED). A read transaction obtains a pointer to the root B-tree page; traversal follows page pointers through the mapped region. No read() syscall, no memory copy, no buffer pool management code. With a 10 GB database and 16 GB RAM, the entire database stays in page cache, and LMDB achieves read latencies of 1–5 μs on a hot working set—close to pure memory access speeds.

examples.title: Redis and THP Interaction
examples.description: Redis deployed with THP enabled on Linux experienced periodic 50–100ms latency spikes in production, correlated with khugepaged activity. The khugepaged daemon moves 4 KB pages into 2 MB huge pages in the background, temporarily holding the process's address space lock. Redis's Redis-5.0 release notes explicitly document the problem and recommend disabling THP. After disabling, the latency spikes disappeared and p99 latency stabilized.

examples.title: llama.cpp Model Inference with mmap
examples.description: llama.cpp loads a 70B model (140 GB) via mmap() with MAP_POPULATE=false. Inference for a single request accesses only the transformer layers needed; the kernel pages in only those layers on first access. On a machine with 24 GB RAM, the first request experiences major page faults as 24 GB of model weights are loaded from an NVMe SSD. Subsequent requests hit the page cache and run near memory speed. The mmap approach makes running models larger than RAM practical at the cost of cold-start latency.

keyTakeaways: Virtual memory's page table + TLB abstraction makes per-process address spaces feasible; TLB pressure from large working sets is a real performance concern
mmap() enables zero-copy file I/O by mapping the page cache into the process's address space; ideal for read-mostly large file access
Major page faults (disk I/O) are production latency events; mlock() and MAP_POPULATE prevent them for latency-critical paths
THP reduces TLB pressure but causes background compaction stalls; disable for Redis, Postgres, MongoDB
vm.swappiness=1 prevents latency-sensitive processes from being swapped to disk under memory pressure
NUMA-aware memory allocation and thread binding prevent 2–3× remote memory access penalties on multi-socket servers
whyItMatters: Virtual memory and mmap are the foundation of how every database, cache, JVM, and ML inference engine manages its memory. The choice between mmap and read() I/O determines who controls eviction. THP and swappiness settings cause mysterious latency spikes in production. NUMA misalignment causes unexplained throughput degradation on large servers. Engineers who understand virtual memory can diagnose these issues, tune kernel parameters correctly, and design systems that use memory efficiently at scale.
reflectionQuestions: Your Redis deployment experiences p99 latency spikes of 80ms every few minutes on a machine with 128 GB RAM and plenty of free memory. Walk through the investigation and likely causes.

Design the memory management strategy for an ML inference server that serves 50 different model versions (each 10 GB) concurrently, with at most 200 GB of RAM. How would you use mmap and the page cache to maximize the effective working set?
Explain why a database that uses mmap() for its data files cannot guarantee strict durability without additional mechanisms. What must be done to make mmap-based writes durable?
numbersToKnow: 4 KB: default Linux page size; 2 MB: huge page size on x86-64
TLB miss cost: 10–50 cycles (page table walk in cache); major page fault: 1–10 ms (disk I/O)
vm.swappiness=1: near-disable swap for latency-sensitive services (Redis, Postgres recommendation)
10–30%: typical JVM throughput improvement after switching to 2 MB huge pages
TLB shootdown: 1–5 μs per CPU core; costly when triggered at high frequency by mmap/munmap

exercises: Write a C program that mmap()s a 1 GB file, measures time to randomly access 100,000 locations (cold), then measures again after the working set is warm. Observe the major page fault count in /proc/self/status (MajFlt) and correlate with the latency difference.

On a Linux machine, observe THP behavior: check /proc/sys/kernel/mm/transparent_hugepage/enabled, run a memory-intensive workload, and observe /proc/vmstat (thp_fault_alloc, thp_collapse_alloc). Then disable THP and re-run; measure latency variance difference.
